title: Brooding chicks with a heat plate
subtitle: A safer alternative to heat lamps for the first six weeks.
excerpt: A heat plate is a flat heated panel that chicks shelter under rather than a lamp they sit beneath. It mimics the hen's body heat more closely than a bare bulb, reduces fire risk, and allows chicks to self-regulate their temperature more naturally. Here is how to set one up and what to watch for in the first six weeks.
sourceNotes: British Hen Welfare Trust, chick brooding guidance. Poultry Club of Great Britain, rearing guidance (2022). National Farmers Union, poultry welfare factsheet.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat, thermostatically controlled panel mounted on legs above the chick litter. Chicks shelter underneath it for warmth, much as they would shelter under a broody hen. Runs at lower surface temperatures than a heat lamp and poses less fire risk.
A condition in young chicks where droppings dry and stick to the vent, blocking it. Can be fatal if not cleared. Common in the first week, often triggered by temperature stress or poor nutrition.

content.text: gives chicks a warm area to retreat to without bathing the whole brooder in heat. Chicks that are too warm simply move away from the plate; chicks that are cold move under it. You get a much clearer picture of the flock's comfort from watching where they choose to stand than from watching a thermometer.
Set the heat plate on its legs at the manufacturer's recommended starting height (usually 3 to 5 cm clearance for day-olds). The underside of the plate should be at the level of the chicks' backs.
Cover the brooder floor with 5 to 7 cm of wood shavings or chopped straw. Do not use newspaper, which is too slippery for chicks' legs in the first week.
Turn on the plate one hour before chicks arrive to let it warm up to temperature.
Place water drinkers and feed stations at the edge of the brooder, not directly under the plate. Chicks should be able to eat and drink without getting hot.
Chicks spread out around the plate and forage actively: temperature is right.
Chicks all crowded under the plate and cheeping loudly: too cold. Raise the plate height or add a draught excluder around the brooder walls.
Chicks avoiding the plate and panting: too hot. Lower the plate height or move it to the corner.
Weeks 1 and 2: raise plate height by 1 cm every two to three days as chicks grow. Check for
daily. Clear any blockage gently with a warm damp cloth.
Weeks 3 and 4: chicks will start spending time away from the plate during the day. Continue raising height as they grow.
Weeks 5 and 6: most breeds are feathered enough to manage without supplemental heat if the air temperature is above 18°C. Turn the plate off for a day and observe before removing it entirely.
